💡 Key Takeaways
  • Critical Virtzilla bugs allow authentication bypass, as a nested virtualization problem got Digital Ocean ducking.
  • If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.
  • Industry observers note that VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this concern to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Critical Virtzilla bugs allow authentication bypass, as a nested virtualization problem got Digital Ocean ducking.

If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.

Industry observers note that VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this concern to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite.

It has been revealed that VMware also wants its users to address CVE-2026-123891, which allows attackers to read and write the database used by SDDC Manager, the tool for managing entire software-defined datacenters. Attackers can execute arbitrary commands and elevate privileges to root.

It has been revealed that the prospect of an unknown party getting access to vCenter or SDDC manager is not pleasant. At least VMware has fixed its software.

The virty giant hasn't done the same to address a second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, which warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618).

VMware looks to ship newly introduced versions of its products with a patched version of Apache, but for now only has workarounds that disable the http2 protocol.

Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours.

This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host.

It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses.

This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts consumers of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5.

Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Terra Security says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs.

Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18.

Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours.

According to recent reports, the Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to patch its Linux implementations. The firm has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE.

The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®.

#46690. Breaking: Persistent incrementality in Rust

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4166 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Persistent incrementality in Rust

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is this cool idea: incremental computations.
  • This concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood.
  • And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is this cool idea: incremental computations. The concept is simple, if you calculated something and then inputs change, it doesn't have to mean that you need to recompute everything. Most of your computations might still be valid, and quite often it is the case that you only need to redo a small chunk of changes.

This concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood. Probably, the most common example is incremental compilation, which makes the compilation reuse as much work as possible, making iterations during development much faster. The interesting part is "iterating": note that incremental compilation doesn't necessarily makes cold builds faster. The compiler performance might be roughly the same with and without incrementality, it's just repeated reuse of compiler artifacts becomes more efficient. Most likely you've heard of it. And if you did, you probably know that incremental compilation is not easy (1, 2, 3). But it's cool!

And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).

Industry observers note that it could be somewhat related to the fact that rust-analyzer uses salsa as the central part of its architecture. Salsa is a library that makes incremental computations very convenient and efficient. There is one drawback, though. It is mainly designed to work in memory. And we'll touch on how it works in a bit.

For project like Rust Glancer that tries to keep the memory usage as low as possible, this doesn't work. Because of that, for a long time Rust Glancer didn't use incremental computations, and instead had a sophisticated network of persistent caches with sharding and targeted optimizations to make computations efficient. And it worked, for a while. But this approach doesn't scale very well: if you need to maintain a manually implemented custom cache format, optimize it, and tie computations to it, then the more efficiency you seek, the more complexity you get. Basically, the complexity is "quadratic": it grows as O(computations_complexity * cache_implementation_complexity) because both are interconnected (sorry, CS purists, for this crime).

So... Rust Glancer got to a point where it would really benefit from persistent incremental computations. And the search for it turned out to be really interesting, so in this blog post we'll be discussing how incremental computations can work in memory and how to make this approach work with persistency.

Before we start discussing how incremental computations work under the hood, let's see how it looks like.

According to recent reports, if you know how to use Salsa feel free to jump to the next section. If you're familiar with red-green algorithm and in-memory approach that Salsa uses, you can skip to where persistency starts.

Now, incremental computations are somewhat tricky to explain in a blog post, because the value of it requires an application to be somewhat massive. So we will need an example that is big enough to show the value of incrementality, but small enough to discuss here. It's a bit absurd, but I hope you can focus on the idea, not on the value of the snippet at hand.

Let's imagine that we're doing a weird text processor that would count the words in all the files in the directory, and decide whether this count is funny. And to make things more interesting, the files can include other files.

Industry observers note that how would that look if implemented naively? Something like that, most likely (well, let's ignore the IO):.

the output will also have no surprises:.

Now, let's try Salsa. It should let us make some computations reusable. Here's how it would look like:.

Recent findings suggest that the code looks pretty similar! However, let's inspect the output.

The first call matches the naive example:.

But the second call is different!

Note: not only we did not call word_count(a), we did not call is_haha_number as well!

Salsa can see that file b changed, and it re-run word_count for it. But the output did not change, so all the previous computations are valid: nothing to be run.

The third output is interesting too:.

The word count in b changed, and a includes b, so we need to re-run all three queries. But the order is inversed! This is because we have a dependency graph internally, and we're walking through the dependency tree and re-execute changed queries from the "leaves" to the "root".

We have changed b from 65 to 67 words, so a now has 69 words. Result is still true, but we did have to revision the computations. If we would've had another query that depended on is_haha_number, that's where validation would've stopped and all the queries above wouldn't need to run.

And the final output is interesting too:.

We have changed dependencies of a, so there is no b anymore. So we start with what we know: word_count for a. It now has a not-yet-tracked dependency on c, so we go to c after a. And the rest is the same.

So I hope you get the idea now: each query result is memorized, and if we discover that the output of this query did not change, we don't need to recompute the queries that depend on this input. Or rather, if all the queries that query X depends on did not change, then query X does not need to be recomputed.

According to recent reports, and now imagine that you have 700 dependencies in your workspace. A single file changed in the topmost dependency. 699 dependencies can keep their result! Within a single crate, still only one file has changed, so the information about all the other files at least partially stays the same. We only need to redo the computations that actually matter.

And most importantly, we don't need to write any of this tracking code ourselves, Salsa gives it to us for free.

According to recent reports, well, it's really not trivial. If you want to have a more formal deep dive, I suggest the following reads:.

Recent findings suggest that imagine that each query, combined with its arguments, is an object. This object can have a bunch of metadata, stating whether it was already computed, when it happened, what was the output, and what's the object dependencies. Let's call this metadata a "memo".

Industry observers note that side note: why is "combined with its arguments?" important? Because we cannot memoize is_haha_number, but we can memoize is_haha_number(420), so you can think of it as a mapping of (function, arguments) -> output.

And imagine that you have inputs: something that user provides, and this something can be explicitly requested by a query.

We might also say that the database has a revision, initially 1. When you change some input, the revision gets bumped to 2, and so on. This revision can be used as "when it happened" (or rather, "when it change last time") inside of the memo.

Industry observers note that now, we've provided our inputs and invoke a query. It has some associated code that can internally do two things:.

If query requests an input, it should record that it depends on this input. So if input changes, it must be recomputed.

If query requests another query, we might check if the corresponding query has a memo with a computed value. If it has, we need to make sure that it is valid for the revision we're at. If it is: great! It can be reused, and we don't need to recompute it. Otherwise, we need to recursively go into this query. Obviously, we also record a dependency on this query.

According to recent reports, during the execution, we'll collect all the inputs and all the dependency queries, and ultimately we'll finally compute the result of our query. And when we do, we can fill out the memo: record the revision and the output.

And... done! Next time you request an output, we will look at this query object memo. If inputs did not change, we can just hand out the result. If they changed, we go down the query line, and do the same thing. So naturally only the things that actually might have changed will be recomputed.

Recent findings suggest that oh, but there is one more key detail here, that makes everything even better. If revision changed, it does not automatically mean that we need to recompute this query. We might recompute dependencies, and compare them to the old values. If all the outputs are the equal to the old ones (imagine that word_count(a) changed from 67 to 69, but is_haha_number still returns true true: the query that depends on is_haha_number might not get invalidated), we can just mark the current version as verified and return the old result. And it can matter a lot when the expensive query has a lot of cheap dependencies.

In a recent development, obviously, it's an overly simplified explanation. In practice, there are many, many caveats, tricky parts, and optimizations that make the experience work well. But my job here is to give you an idea; if you've become interested in the topic, I'd recommend looking to Salsa source code, it's very interesting.

Industry observers note that and Salsa is awesome! With one caveat. It works in memory only. Well, there is ongoing work on persistency there, but AFAIU it is mostly focused on storing the computations on filesystem so that they can be reloaded later (snapshot-like). It is very valuable, but we still have to store stuff in the memory. For the project like Rust Glancer we want to offload stuff to occupy less RAM.

And in practice, there are several projects that do implement various kinds of persistence:.

So there are solutions for this problem, but none of them seem to be "Salsa but everything is on the filesystem".

I guess then it would be fine to build one?

It has been revealed that as you probably guessed, I did build one. And I called it Ajika. And I'm very proud of myself for coming up with this name, yes.

In a recent development, the library is here, it uses stable Rust, and is generally a complete project (but I'm working on improvements!). The post, however, is not meant to promote it; obviously it's a very young library, and while so far it works really well for me, probably sticking to Salsa if it works for you is a safe choice. Not gonna sell it, do your own research :).

What I want to share is how Ajika works under the hood and what makes it different from Salsa.

But (spoiler) in general it's just two things:.

And we'll get to it and see how it works, but to make everything clear, we'll need to start from something very basic.

Here's the same program we had for Salsa, but migrated to Ajika:.

It looks pretty similar, with API changes mostly being a taste difference, and on a first run it has the same output.

However, the key part here is that we can add the following to the end:.

Recent findings suggest that and print_result will just print False. Nothing will be executed after restart! Persistency in action!

It has been revealed that on a serious note, the main difference is the focus. When you start working on a project like that, choosing your priority can influence the design a lot. And the choice made here is being persistent-first. While Ajika provides an in-memory backend, it's mostly meant for tests. The intended use case is to use your disk.

And it starts with a very basic question that in-memory database does not have: what happens if I restart the application?

If you already have a cache locally, many things can make this cache invalid:.

And similarly, given that we cache computations, it's basically an optimization. If cache gets corrupted or removed while the application is running, user would most likely prefer the cache to be discarded and computations to be repeated one more time, rather than the app crashing with "cache is not available, what do I do???".

In a recent development, as a result, the cache must be throw-away. Both Ajika and application supply schema versions to identify the revision, and if the stored cache doesn't match it, we reset it. If cache gets corrupted, Ajika will attempt recovery over hard failing, even if it means re-computing data from scratch.

Sources indicate that the next most noticeable change is that most operations are fallible. Since IO is the basic property for us, and IO can fail, we need to think about it. Failed operation does not mean that cache is corrupted, but it does mean that the current query might not be computed. Typically, it can be retried, though.

In a recent development, finally, the persistence is, unfortunately, a leaky abstraction. You cannot really hide from the fact that the data is outside of memory, because everything you persist must be serializable. And your interim query data might be reusable but not serializable (imagine an AST that borrows the source text: making it own the data likely will be worse), so some of the queries might be transient: we compute them once and retain while the current operation runs, but drop instead of persisting once operation ends.

Together, these properties start working rather nicely, however: your application has to be aware of persistence, but not in an annoying way. If something fails, you know about it, but you don't have to worry, since Ajika will repair things for you. If something is not serializable and it doesn't matter, it can be turned into a transient query. If you don't want your tests to rely on persistence, you just plug a memory backend in.

So let's take a look at how it works under the hood.

LLM usage disclaimer: The library discussed here is developed with use of LLMs, same as Rust Glancer. Hopefully, from this post it is evident that I'm using LLMs as a tool and have full control. It's not vibe coded.

There are three parts to Ajika: ajika itself, ajika_macros, and ajika_storage.

Sources indicate that we'll take a look at ajika and then at ajika_storage. Macros are left as an exercise to a reader, but they're generally pretty straightforward.

Ajika itself is very easy, just check out this diagram:.

...just kidding. But we'll fix that very quickly.

The core idea is very similar to Salsa:.

Still, I think it might be useful to skim through the high level details.

It has been revealed that side note: Ajika has its own book which does a much deeper dive on many concepts than this blog post. I'll be referring to it in some places. The con is that, unlike this handwritten blog post, the text there is mostly LLM-generated, and even if I did a lot of polishing, it shows. Eventually I'll do a full manual rewrite, but for now I figured that human-filtered-llm-guide is better than no guide at all.

Recent findings suggest that database is an entrypoint. You choose either an in-memory or persistent backend, supply Inputs and then run your operation.

Queries are the actual logic we want to execute. They are defined via ajika::query macro and in general pretty straightforward. More details on queries themselves are in the book, and we'll look at how queries are executed and what this Db object is a bit later in this post.

Inputs are somewhat more interesting. Your input type is defined through the ajika::input procedural macro, which would do some wrapping for you. And your input structure is basically a mapping: you specify a key, for example, String, and then you can use database to get an input value (or lack thereof) for whatever key you have, be it "foo" or even "bar". If you have a singleton value, like a config, you can use () as a key. Again, more on inputs can be found in the book, also might check out lazy inputs.

Outputs are probably the first part of the system that gets interesting because of persistence.

According to recent reports, the outputs need to be stored on the filesystem, so they need to be serializable. For outputs that you don't want to serialize, you can use transient queries which will keep the value in memory only for the duration of a single operation. But even then, there is a problem: how significant of an output do you want?

If you will have a 1000 very granular queries, it will mean that we need a lot of filesystem roundtrips. If you will have just a bunch of queries that compute a ton of data, you will need to deserialize a major value just to look at the part of it.

Industry observers note that thus, outputs offer a solution that lies in between: you can choose to return a value directly, or return a handle to this value. If you return a handle, query can use this handle to retrieve the value from the database on demand. Directly returned values are fully deserialized. This offers you a nice granularity option: you have a query that encapsulates a meaningful unit of work, but it returns you an object that contains handles for particular results. Handle is cheap to obtain and deserialize, and you only query the data you actually need. Doing is most convenient through an ajika::output macro.

As usual, more details on how to use outputs are in the book.

And now we're getting to the interesting stuff.

To perform a single run we need three things:.

And there are two related concepts that make things work:.

Recent findings suggest that record contains information like values metadata for a query and dependencies for it (note: values are stored separately!). Thus, Memos are released on the end of the run and then later can be reconstructed from Record on demand.

And this is an important bit: released memos don't occupy RAM. This is the key part of Ajika! During the query execution, the values can be loaded, but if you don't run any operations, you don't have to pay for it. Outputs will just wait for you inside of the filesystem! Moreover, whenever we run queries, we only load what we need, not everything.

Each time a query logic actually runs (either from run or from another query), a fresh Db with a new Frame is created, sharing the same Operation.

When you ask Db to execute a query, here's a typical (overly simplified) workflow:.

And if during execution query receives another query result, it records it in its own Frame for reuse.

Obviously, there is a lot of bookkeeping, support for parallelism, and other things that make it complex, but in general the algorithm is pretty straightforward.

Industry observers note that once the operation finishes, we need to actually apply the changes. run works as a transaction, so everything that was done inside is immediately visible, but after run depending on whether run failed or succeeded, the results will either be discarded or persisted.

Checkpoint write is generally pretty straightforward:.

So checkpoint on the Ajika level is pretty straightforward. What is more interesting is how Ajika storage works in general.

Finally, we've got to the persistence!

Industry observers note that it's probably the most interesting part of Ajika. How do we store data in a way that is efficient?

It has been revealed that the first version of Ajika used redb for everything. It worked, but it did not work very well. Since we don't really have a "database" per se, and more of a storage for many blobs, redb added too much overhead. However, it provides much needed features like transactions.

So, Ajika uses redb as a metadata storage: it's an index which mostly contains pointers to the values.

The values are written in "pack files": basically, just binary files to which we can append latest entries. And inside of redb we can just store a pointer: (file name, offset). Each stored entry has a header with information such as length and compression algorithm. For efficiency, if the value is very small, we can keep it inline inside of redb instead of writing it to a file.

If you want to access a value, you will go to redb, check the corresponding key, and then either read it inline or read the specified pack at the specified access. Pretty simple.

Obviously, there is some more data stored there (we'll talk about identities soon, briefly), but in general it's a pretty "stupid" (hopefully in a good way) format of data storage.

According to recent reports, however, there is one caveat: if we do it naively, the storage can grow without limits. Packs can end up with very low utilization factor, consisting mostly of "dead" values, and some of them might not be observable at all. So the storage supports maintenance: whenever you do an operation, Ajika might do a sweep that would re-pack values and revision pointers, and at the end of operation Ajika will try to signal to the storage which values can be removed now. There are a few knobs you can tune here: you can specify the retention limit time (so that the very old and unused queries are cleaned up) or target storage size (which acts as a soft limit, and will affect the cleanup policy).

But ultimately, this design makes value storing and retrieval pretty efficient, and it integrates with the overall Ajika design very well.

OK, we're almost done, I promise! The last small bit: interning.

In a recent development, interning values is an optimization that gives you a way to turn any object into an ID. Imagine that you have file paths. They can work as IDs, but it would probably be more efficient if you used FileId(0) / FileId(1) instead. Not only in terms of performance, but often also in terms of memory: you'd rather not have a ton of strings in memory if you don't really need them. Sometimes, interning strings on its own can be a very useful memory optimization, which is why crates like string_cache exist.

But for us, having IDs for objects can be valuable in general, because your computations results might often be linked to some other objects, and it's useful to be able to use IDs for that.

According to recent reports, salsa supports interning for that purpose, and Ajika does it too. However, there is one caveat for Ajika: what happens if we have our IDs allocated, they become a part of the cache, and then we restart the application?

To avoid this problem, IDs in Ajika are persisted in addition to being stored in memory, and on restart this interner state is reloaded.

Sources indicate that ajika development itself was an experiment: I did not create it in vacuum, I was actually porting Rust Glancer to it at the same time. And the experiment was very successful. I was able to remove a lot of complexity from Rust Glancer, and Ajika unblocked many optimizations that were not realistic with hand-rolled caches (starting with lazy body evaluation).

At the end of the experiment, Rust Glancer got performance comparable to rust-analyzer (sometimes even better!). Ajika is obviously slower than salsa, but inside of IDE the difference between 1 and 30ms is negligible, both feel instant. What matters is the low RAM usage: Rust Glancer still stays well under 100MB RAM idle on pretty big projects.

Remark: exact comparison between two will be posted in the release notes for Rust Glancer 0.5.0, so stay tuned.

It has been revealed that as the experiments go, the branch of Rust Glancer where all of that happened is in a half-assembled state, and it's way too rushed and "prototyped" to just merge it, so I'm doing a clean reimplementation using extracted (and published) version of Ajika. It will take a while, but I'm very excited: Rust Glancer without compromises that feels instant and does not eat memory.

Thanks for reading, it turned out to be a long post. A lot of effort went into it, so I hope that it was useful, at least somewhat.

My next goal is to prepare an Ajika-based release of Rust Glancer, and after that I have a lot of ideas on how to make Ajika even faster/better/stronger. Who knows, maybe it will eventually grow into a product of its own, not merely a part of Rust Glancer ecosystem.

As usual, the best way to support if you like the project is to check out Rust Glancer, star Ajika (but only if you like it!) and/or follow me on twitter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs.
  • The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.
  • That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs.

The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.

That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.

The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items.

BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance.

But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent.

Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies, the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security.

Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft.

Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons.

The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The Newly introduced York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation.

Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law.

One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.”.

Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk.

Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions.

Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact.

Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow.

Industry observers note that alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the latest policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.”.

“Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure initiative,” he noted.

But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the fresh policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028.

Alibaba’s Wu predicted his firm “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed.

Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors.

And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments.

That’s likely because Beijing needs to approve imports and chose not to do so while its own chipmakers develop improved products. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn.

Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.

Sources indicate that linkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure. The deployment reduces daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20, lowers compute costs by 10%, and improves application runtimes by 14%, compared with its previous Magnet implementation.

Daily shuffle fetch failures decreased from approximately 750 to 20 (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post).

LinkedIn's offline data platform executes more than 300,000 Spark jobs daily across thousands of production nodes, consuming approximately 200 petabyte-hours of compute. As the company moves toward a unified Flink architecture for real-time and historical processing, large-scale backfills introduce additional shuffle workloads. Shuffle moves intermediate data between processing stages, potentially stressing networks, disks, and application runtimes.

LinkedIn previously addressed shuffle read inefficiencies with Magnet, its push-based shuffle implementation contributed to Apache Spark 3.2. Magnet aggregates shuffle blocks by reducer partition into larger files, reducing random disk reads. However, shuffle storage remained within the compute cluster, where External Shuffle Services shared CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network resources with compute workloads.

According to recent reports, with Apache Celeborn, map tasks push intermediate data to dedicated workers, which aggregate and store partitions independently of compute executors. Reducers fetch the data directly from these workers, allowing shuffle storage to scale independently of compute and reducing dependence on executor lifecycles. Unlike Magnet, which uses merger External Shuffle Services within the Spark compute cluster, Celeborn runs as a separate shuffle service with dedicated workers and a replicated control plane. This separation reduces resource contention between compute and shuffle workloads.

Celeborn architecture at LinkedIn (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post).

Aravind Patnam, a staff software engineer at LinkedIn, explained,.

Operating it reliably across thousands of nodes and hundreds of thousands of daily applications required substantial engineering beyond the upstream project.

The deployment uses a five-node Raft-based control plane distributed across availability zones, with Apache Ratis providing metadata replication, leader election, and failover. LinkedIn also introduced network-aware replication and integrated Celeborn with its host health platform to deprioritize workers approaching maintenance and exclude degraded workers. These changes contributed to a 20-fold reduction in task failures during infrastructure disruptions compared with Magnet.

LinkedIn further optimized the data plane by moving shuffle storage to NVMe SSDs, reducing overall shuffle duration by 40%. Using Zstandard compression instead of LZ4 reduced the required shuffle worker fleet by approximately 35%. The company also provisioned workers with 100 Gbps network interfaces and improved slot selection time sixfold through JVM and data-plane optimizations. Across the fleet, shuffle cost decreased by nearly 90% per task, while the proportion of executor runtime spent waiting on shuffle operations fell by approximately 10–15% from its peak.

Industry observers note that the converged Flink platform processes hundreds of millions of events per hour in historical backfills, completing multi-day workloads in single-digit hours. Thousands of pipelines now use unified Flink computations for nearline processing and historical corrections, replacing parallel Spark implementations. LinkedIn is exploring caching and faster upstream upgrades while continuing to contribute to Celeborn.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier.

  • According to recent reports, as a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

In a recent development, building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

According to recent reports, as a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Initiative, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that see if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful initiative, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation initiative.

Industry observers note that what took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable proposal, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped challenges, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

You’re ready to turn that strategy into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

It has been revealed that writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

Sources indicate that after spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Industry observers note that your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

It has been revealed that figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up problems, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

Recent findings suggest that take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

According to recent reports, you don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”.

Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a major part of that.
  • Industry observers note that this is where we are right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a major part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

Industry observers note that this is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

In a recent development, GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

Recent findings suggest that we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

Industry observers note that no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

Recent findings suggest that transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

In a recent development, the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Industry observers note that transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

Sources indicate that llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for latest architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

Industry observers note that the kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

In a recent development, the first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Recent findings suggest that faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

According to recent reports, these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

Recent findings suggest that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

In a recent development, if you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an problem with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • It has been revealed that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • In a recent development, as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly crucial sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

It has been revealed that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

In a recent development, as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly crucial sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

It has been revealed that transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Recent findings suggest that performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Sources indicate that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

Sources indicate that the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

According to recent reports, once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Industry observers note that reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

  • BEUC said: "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BEUC urges Brussels to impose tougher penalties over alleged barriers to switching services and controlling personal data.

Significant Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.

BEUC said: "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products.".

The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023, imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition.

Industry observers note that the devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on.

Sources indicate that BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026.

According to recent reports, in the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the tech giant used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from people for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine.

"Microsoft also regularly prompts owners who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC stated.

Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store owners to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications.

The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge people into handing over their data.

Apple announced fresh terms for developers earlier this year in response to its App Store dispute with the European Commission, but BEUC remarked it was "concerned that the new terms do not resolve fundamental non-compliance complications.".

Google did not respond to requests for comment from The Register. A Microsoft spokesperson told us: "We are continuing to engage with the Commission and industry at large to ensure Microsoft's designated platforms comply fully with the DMA.".

An Amazon spokesperson told The Register “Our consent experience is clear and gives customers informed choice about how their personal information is used across Amazon services. We see that in practice.

“A seller that uses Amazon Stores in the EU can offer the same products on any third-party online marketplace or its own direct to customer website at any price, without affecting their eligibility to be highlighted as the Featured Offer. This is set out clearly in our DMA Compliance Report.”.

Sources indicate that BEUC director general Agustín Reyna said: "The era of cosmetic compliance must end. It is high time the Commission holds gatekeepers to account and imposes dissuasive penalties in all cases where they bypass the DMA's rules.".

Recent findings suggest that the report has been shared with the Commission. Whether BEUC's allegations lead to further findings of non-compliance or penalties is now a matter for the regulator. ®.
